{{short description|Concept in geometry including line and circle}}
In [[geometry]], a '''generalised circle''', sometimes called a ''cline'' or ''circline'',<ref>
{{cite book |last=Hitchman |first=Michael P. |year=2009 |title=Geometry with an Introduction to Cosmic Topology |publisher=Jones & Bartlett |page=43 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yveG5B1few4C&pg=PA43 }}</ref> is a [[straight line]] or a [[circle]], the [[curve]]s of constant [[curvature]] in the [[Euclidean plane]].

The natural setting for generalised circles is the extended plane, a [[plane (geometry)|plane]] along with one [[point at infinity]] through which every straight line is considered to pass. Given any three distinct points in the extended plane, there exists precisely one generalised circle passing through all three.

Generalised circles sometimes appear in [[Euclidean geometry]], which has a well-defined notion of [[Euclidean distance|distance]] between points, and where every circle has a center and radius: the point at infinity can be considered infinitely distant from any other point, and a line can be considered as a [[degeneracy (mathematics)|degenerate]] circle without a well-defined center and with infinite radius (zero [[curvature]]). A [[reflection (mathematics)|reflection]] across a line is a Euclidean [[isometry]] (distance-preserving transformation) which maps lines to lines and circles to circles; but an [[inversion in a circle]] is not, distorting distances and mapping any line to a circle passing through the reference circles's center, and vice-versa.

However, generalised circles are fundamental to [[inversive geometry]], in which circles and lines are considered indistinguishable, the point at infinity is not distinguished from any other point, and the notions of curvature and distance between points are ignored. In inversive geometry, reflections, inversions, and more generally their [[Function composition|compositions]], called [[Möbius transformation]]s, map generalised circles to generalised circles, and preserve the inversive relationships between objects.
 
The extended plane can be identified with the [[sphere]] using a [[stereographic projection]]. The point at infinity then becomes an ordinary point on the sphere, and all generalised circles become circles on the sphere.

==Extended complex plane==
[[File:Circle in the complex plane.png|thumb|upright=1.25|A circle in the complex plane specified as an implicit equation in terms of center and radius]]
The extended Euclidean plane can be identified with the [[extended complex plane]], so that equations of [[complex number]]s can be used to describe lines, circles and inversions.

=== Bivariate linear equation ===

A [[circle]] <math>\Gamma</math> is the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of [[Point (geometry)|points]] <math>z</math>  in a plane that lie at [[radius]] <math>r</math> from a center point <math>\gamma.</math>

:<math>\Gamma(\gamma, r) = \{ z : \text{the distance between } z \text{ and } \gamma \text{ is } r \} </math>

In the [[complex plane]], <math>\gamma</math> is a complex number and <math>\Gamma</math> is a set of complex numbers. Using the property that a complex number multiplied by its [[complex conjugate|conjugate]] is the square of its [[Absolute value#Complex numbers|modulus]] (its [[Euclidean distance]] from the origin), an [[implicit equation]] for <math>\Gamma</math> is:

:<math>\begin{align}
r^2 &= \left| z - \gamma \right|^2 = (z-\gamma)\overline{(z-\gamma)} \\[5mu]
0 &= z \bar z - \bar \gamma z - \gamma \bar z + \left(\gamma \bar \gamma - r^2\right).
\end{align}</math>

This is a [[homogeneous equation|homogeneous]] [[bivariate polynomial|bivariate]] [[linear polynomial]] equation in terms of the complex variable <math>z</math> and its conjugate <math>\bar{z},</math> of the form

:<math>
A z \bar z + B z + C \bar z + D = 0,
</math>

where [[coefficient]]s <math>A</math> and <math>D</math> are [[real number|real]], and <math>B</math> and <math>C</math> are [[complex conjugate]]s.

By dividing by <math>A</math> and then reversing the steps above, the radius <math>r</math> and center <math>\gamma</math> can be recovered from any equation of this form. The equation represents a generalised circle in the plane when <math>r</math> is real, which occurs when <math>AD < BC</math> so that the squared radius <math>r^2 = (BC - AD)/A^2</math> is positive. When <math>A</math> is zero, the equation defines a straight line.

=== Complex reciprocal ===
That the reciprocal transformation <math>z \mapsto w = 1/z</math> maps generalised circles to generalised circles is straight-forward to verify:

:<math>\begin{align}
0 &= A z \bar z + B z + C \bar z + D \\[5mu]
&= \frac{A}{w\bar w} + \frac{B}{w} + \frac{C}{\bar w} + D \\[5mu]
&= A  + B \bar w + C w + D w \bar w  \\[5mu]
&= D \bar w w + C w + B \bar w + A .
\end{align}</math>

Lines through the origin {{nobr|(<math>A = D = 0</math>)}} map to lines through the origin; lines not through the origin {{nobr|(<math>A = 0, D \neq 0</math>)}} map to circles through the origin; circles through the origin {{nobr|(<math>A \neq 0, D =0</math>)}} map to lines not through the origin; and circles not through the origin {{nobr|(<math>A \neq 0, D \neq 0</math>)}} map to circles not through the origin.

=== Complex matrix representation ===
The defining equation of a generalised circle 

:<math>0 = A z \bar z + B z + C \bar z + D</math>

can be written as a matrix equation

:<math>
0 = \begin{pmatrix}z & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\bar{z} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.
</math>

Symbolically,

:<math>0 = \mathbf{z}^\text{T} \mathfrak C \, \bar{\mathbf{z}},</math>

with coefficients placed into an [[invertible matrix|invertible]] [[hermitian matrix]] <math>\mathfrak C = {\mathfrak C}^\dagger</math> representing the circle, and <math>\mathbf{z} = \begin{pmatrix} z & 1 \end{pmatrix}^\text{T}</math> a vector representing an extended complex number.

Two such matrices specify the same generalised circle [[if and only if]] one is a [[scalar multiplication|scalar multiple]] of the other.

To transform the generalised circle represented by <math>\mathfrak C</math> by the [[Möbius transformation]] <math>\mathfrak H,</math> apply the inverse of the Möbius transformation <math>\mathfrak G = \mathfrak H^{-1}</math> to the vector <math>\mathbf{z}</math> in the implicit equation,

:<math>\begin{align}
0 &= \left({\mathfrak G} \mathbf{z}\right)^\text{T}
\mathfrak C \,
\overline{(
  \mathfrak G
  \mathbf{z}
)} \\ [5mu]
&= 
\mathbf{z}^\text{T}
\left({\mathfrak G}^\text{T} \mathfrak C \bar{\mathfrak G} \right)
\bar{\mathbf{z}},
\end{align}</math>

so the new circle can be represented by the matrix <math>{\mathfrak G}^\text{T} {\mathfrak C} \bar{\mathfrak G}.</math>
